question: Does a gradient-boosting model using upstream stop delays and the leading vehicle's delay predict downstream transit delays better than a standard per-vehicle travel-time regression on a simulated bus line?
method: Numpy simulation of one bus route with delay propagation, headway recovery, peaks and noise; time-ordered train/test split by day; baseline linear regression vs grouped-CV-tuned LightGBM.

dataset.name: Simulated single bus route (numpy, generated in analysis.py)

baseline: Per-vehicle linear regression of downstream arrival delay on the vehicle's own last observed delay and scheduled time at the target stop.
improved: LightGBM regressor (CV-tuned on training days) adding delays at all upstream observed stops, leader delays and headways at observed stops, stop index and time of day.
notes: Simulated data, so results reflect the simulator's assumptions, not a real transit agency. Leader delays are used only at observed stops. Baseline is deterministic; improved is averaged over LightGBM seeds 42-44. Late flag = delay above 3 minutes. Single simulated dataset (seed 42).
